messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes 
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)
- Forbidden causal connections that must never appear

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT include inactive components — these are clinically irrelevant for this patient and must not be mentioned.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- For forbidden pairs, never use explicit causal language between them in a single sentence:
  "led to", "caused", "as a result of", "because of", "driven by", "resulting in".
  Both components may appear in the same paragraph — just not causally linked in one sentence.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Animator
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Maladaptive Strategies: Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Memory
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nikolai had been working late in his studio apartment one evening, finalizing frames for an animation deadline, when two men he had barely noticed in the hallway forced their way in and assaulted him. What stayed with him most was not only the fear in the room but the way his body had locked in place on the floor, one arm twisted under him, breath knocked thin and shallow while he tried not to make a sound. In the weeks afterward, he found that certain images could pull him straight back into that moment: the hiss and orange flare of fire on a stove burner or in a movie preview, the sight of needles, IV tubing, or other medical equipment in a clinic, and even reminders of victims in news stories or online posts. When those things appeared, he would immediately put on loud music or turn up the television to drown out the image, or tell himself it could have been worse and force himself not to get angry about what happened. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place and that people were not what they seemed, and he felt as though his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed.

The memories themselves were unlike ordinary recollection. When the assault came to mind, Nikolai said it felt more vivid than memories of everyday life, as if the scene had more texture and force than anything from his usual days at work. He would also feel his body in the same position as when the frightening event occurred, as though his shoulders had seized up again and the pressure of the floor was back under him. Those moments of remembering made him look around with immediate alarm, and he became intensely afraid that someone might be coming for him again. He frequently checked behind him while walking home from his animation studio, especially at night after a long shift, and sudden movements by strangers on the sidewalk or in the lobby put him instantly on guard. He always identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, scanning exits in cafés, the subway, and even the small screening room where he reviewed work with colleagues. Once he had seen how quickly the attack had taken shape, he began to watch other people as though they might change without warning.

That watchfulness kept the event alive in a different way. The more he monitored the street, the more the memory seemed to return with bodily force, and the more often it did, the more he felt compelled to distract himself, shut down anger, and compare his suffering with what could have happened to someone else. On bad evenings he would sit in his apartment with loud music blaring or the TV on for hours, telling himself his injuries had been minor compared with what others endured, while carefully refusing to let himself feel rage toward the men or toward the fact that he had not been able to stop them. Yet those efforts never left him settled for long. When the memories became especially vivid, they brought the same physical posture and helplessness back into his awareness, and that in turn sharpened his suspicion that danger could appear anywhere and that he had to keep looking over his shoulder. By then, he had started crossing streets to avoid groups of men, lingering near doors, and planning every route home around how quickly he could get out if someone moved too fast.

Over months, this pattern narrowed his life. He still went to work as an animator, but the studio had become another place where his vigilance never fully switched off, especially when coworkers moved suddenly behind him or when a project required him to review emergency or medical imagery for accuracy. Fire in an animated scene, even when it was only an effect on a screen, could set off the same surge of unease that sent him reaching for distraction and scanning his surroundings. He was increasingly isolated, single and living alone, and he noticed that his tiredness and irritability were less about the workload than about how much energy it took to keep the fear contained. He finally sought help when he realized he was spending more time checking exits and looking behind him than paying attention to his life, and he feared that if he did not understand what was happening, the memories would keep pulling him back into that position on the floor. What he hoped for was simple but urgent: to feel safe enough to walk home, work, and sleep without constantly bracing for the next sudden movement.
